title: Handcuffs and Backup Centers
brief: Which backups would step into a big role if the starter ahead of them misses time, and which of them have value on their own? It must explain that in our daily league with 2 bench spots most handcuffs are waiver pickups, not draft stashes.
summary: In our 12-team daily league with only 2 bench spots, most handcuffs belong on waivers. Pick them up with FAB the day the starter goes down, not stash them at the auction. Spend a 1 to 3 USD last pick only on backups who already help in some categories, or who are clear one-for-one backups who would start and play 30-plus minutes.

sections.heading: What counts as a handcuff for us

paragraphs.text: A fantasy football handcuff can be worthless until the starter gets hurt. A basketball handcuff is different. He has to help you on his own and also have big upside if the starter misses time. In our league, a backup who does nothing in any of the 9 categories while the starter plays is just a wasted roster spot.

The best case is a clear one-for-one backup. That is a player who would start and play 30-plus minutes if the man ahead of him got hurt. The fewer players ahead of him in the rotation, the fewer injuries it takes for his minutes to rise. If he needs several teammates to get hurt, he is not a must-draft player.

Do not assume a backup point guard is a handcuff. On teams with several ball handlers, wings can take over the role. Role players with upside can still gain when a teammate sits, because their usage goes up. The notes give McDaniels as an example.

sections.heading: Why most handcuffs are waiver pickups here

paragraphs.text: We have 2 bench spots and set lineups every day. Every bench spot should hold someone who helps your categories this week. If you stash a backup who only pays off after an injury, you play a man short in your daily rotation until that injury happens. Several notes call players who only pay off when someone else gets hurt poor late picks. They also say you should not rely on upside that depends on someone else's injury.

Waivers run daily on a FAB budget, with up to 6 adds per week. When a starter goes down, his backup is usually available the next day. So keep some FAB after the auction for these adds, and leave a roster spot you can drop. The 4 IL spots also help: an injured starter can move to IL, which frees a spot for his replacement.

At the auction, a handcuff is worth a 1 to 3 USD final pick only if he has a realistic path to minutes now, or helps in a few categories as he is. One more option: a late pick can insure a star you already own if you take a teammate who would start in the star's place. Make this move with your last dollars, never before your starters are filled.

The experts split on stashing backups late. One side says backups who are one injury away from starting are valid late fliers. They add that a backup big with strong per-minute production is worth drafting because he jumps in value when the starter sits. The other side says late upside picks need a realistic path to a role, and that players who only pay off after an injury are poor late picks. For our 144-player draft, the two views can fit together. Use your final 1 USD pick only on a one-for-one backup with real per-minute production or a role now. Leave everyone else on waivers.

One note says a backup center is not worth rostering until the starter ahead of him is out. Once he starts, he can be an elite streamer. In our daily league, that means you add him the day the starter is ruled out and drop him when the starter returns.

Watch backup center battles behind injury-prone starters, because whoever wins those starts has fantasy value. A backup big who can play back-to-backs, and whose minutes go up when the starter is hurt, is more reliable than a big with his own injury limits. Backup centers also pick up extra minutes on nights when the starter is in foul trouble or not scoring.

Do not draft a backup center just to wait for the starter to be traded. This is usually a waste, especially if he is not a strong per-minute producer. If a trade happens before our 2027-03-04 deadline, use FAB on him then.

sections.heading: What to check in the first weeks

paragraphs.text: For every handcuff on your watch list, check three things early. First, the starter's health and injury status. Second, whether the backup already plays close to 30 minutes or is stuck near 15 to 20. Third, how many players sit ahead of him. If a starter goes out for more than a few days, bid FAB right away. If the backup has only a short spot-start window, add him only for those game days. Our playoffs are weeks 19 to 21 and end on 2027-03-28, so a backup with a strong schedule in those weeks is worth more late in the season.
